# Call for Alaska Birth Defects Registry Advisory Committee Members

## About the Registry

The Alaska Birth Defects Registry (ABDR) is a population-based public health surveillance system that monitors the incidence of birth defects among children under age three throughout Alaska. ABDR plays a critical role in identifying, analyzing, and responding to patterns of birth defects across Alaska’s diverse communities. Approximately 50 birth defects are reportable to ABDR, including the 47 recommended by the [National Birth Defects Prevention Network](https://nbdpn.org/). The registry was established in 1996 and is operated by the [Alaska Division of Public Health](https://health.alaska.gov/en/division-of-public-health/).

## Advisory Committee

The Registry is seeking a group of key stakeholders, senior leaders, and subject-matter experts to provide high-level oversight, guidance, and strategic direction. The aim is for the committee to be a multi-disciplinary body composed of a mix of governmental leaders, technical experts, and community stakeholders.

Examples of membership can be categorized into five core areas:

### 1. Public Health & Governmental Leadership

These individuals will be members of the State of Alaska, Division of Public Health, who help ensure that birth defect surveillance operates within the government's capacity and will have the greatest authority and liability for the registry.

### 2. Technical & Data Governance Experts

With the shift toward "Data Modernization," these roles are critical for the infrastructure of the surveillance system. Individuals may have a background in healthcare data interoperability, be members of the Alaska HIE Healtheconnect, or be data modernization experts or informatics specialists.

### 3. Clinical & Laboratory Partners

Since most of ABDR’s surveillance data originates in healthcare entities, it is important to include clinical representation, such as physicians or nurses who can provide medical expertise, or liaisons from hospital systems who manage the reporting burden and can speak to the feasibility of data collection.

### 4. Legal, Privacy, and Regulatory Experts

Public health surveillance often involves sensitive patient data, making legal expertise helpful for a committee.

### 5. Community & Policy Stakeholders

Patient advocates, members of applicable local non-profits, and individuals with lived expertise can help ensure the surveillance program remains transparent and serves the public interest.

## Member Time Commitment

Semi-Annual Meetings: Committee members can expect 2 main meetings per year, each lasting 1 hour. All meetings will be held via Zoom/Teams.

Preparation: Members will often be expected to spend some time reviewing "meeting packets" (meeting agenda information, technical reports, data privacy drafts) sent out 1–2 weeks before the meeting.

Ad Hoc Consultation: Occasional emails or brief surveys may be sent to all or select committee members.

## Become a Member

The primary purpose of this committee is to ensure that the ABDR remains aligned with organizational goals, stays on track, and delivers the desired outcomes. If you feel like you may be able to help guide and advise the strategic direction of the ABDR, please contact us at **hssbirthdefreg@alaska.gov**
